Practical guidance

Hinge questions

A pre-planned diagnostic question at a critical point where the class response determines whether teaching moves on, consolidates or reteaches.

On this pageImplementation sequenceCheck for impact

What it is: A pre-planned diagnostic question at a critical point where the class response determines whether teaching moves on, consolidates or reteaches.

Why it helps: Plausible distractors reveal specific misconceptions, providing more useful information than a simple right/wrong check and allowing a rapid whole-class decision.

Use it when: after a key concept, before a dependent step and before students move into independent practice.

Implementation sequence

Identify the precise concept on which later learning depends.

Write a clear stem and one defensible correct answer.

Create plausible distractors, each linked to a known misconception.

Collect simultaneous independent responses within a short time.

Ask students to explain choices where needed, then make the planned instructional decision.

Use a related follow-up to verify the response.

DODON'T
Keep options balanced in length and free from accidental clues. Plan in advance what each response pattern will trigger. Use ABCD cards, fingers or whiteboards so everyone commits. Use trivial recall that does not genuinely affect the lesson route. Include joke or obviously implausible distractors. Discuss so long that the question ceases to be an efficient hinge.

Check for impact

Each distractor corresponds to an interpretable misconception.

The next teaching move follows the response pattern, not the original timetable.

Sources informing this profile: DistilED: Hinge Questions; StepFinder: Create Hinge Questions.
